I farm 66 mu here in Quzhou County. That's a good-sized piece of land — big enough that I need to think about efficiency, but every yuan I spend still matters. I've been at this for 6 years now, and I learned mostly by doing and by watching what works for the neighbors around me. I went to middle school, so I can read a fertilizer bag and I went to a training session once at the township office, but at the end of the day I trust what I saw with my own eyes in the field.

My land is split into three blocks. The biggest block, 40 mu, is my wheat-maize rotation — that's the backbone of my farm, same as everyone else around here. I also keep 13 mu in stevia and 13 mu in sweet potato. The stevia brings better money per mu, but it is picky and needs a lot of water and spraying. Sweet potato is steady and doesn't ask for much.

For **winter wheat** on my 40 mu, I will plant **Luyuan 502**. That's what my neighbors plant and they got good yields last year. I do rotary tillage before sowing — I hire a tractor service for that, 40 yuan per mu. For fertilizer, I learned that you can't cheap out on wheat. I will put down **18 kg of nitrogen per mu**, **11 kg of phosphorus per mu**, and **4 kg of potassium per mu**. Half the N goes down as basal with the compound fertilizer, and I topdress the rest at jointing stage when I can see the crop is responding. I have a well, so I will irrigate **4 times** — winter irrigation once, then three more times at green-up, jointing, and grain filling. I spray pesticide **4 times**: herbicide once after sowing, then insecticide twice and fungicide once when the weather turns humid. I expect about **500 kg per mu** if the spring doesn't dry out too bad.

For **summer maize** on that same 40 mu, I will sow **Denghai 605** right after the wheat harvest. Everyone here uses Denghai 605 — it's a hybrid seed, costs a bit more, but the yield is reliable. I plant no-tillage directly into the wheat stubble. The soil is still loose enough and it saves me 40 yuan per mu on tillage costs. I will use **12 kg nitrogen per mu**, **3.5 kg phosphorus per mu**, and **3.5 kg potassium per mu**. I put compound fertilizer down at sowing and side-dress urea at the big trumpet leaf stage. I irrigate **2 times** — once if it is dry at sowing, and once at the tasseling-silking stage. That timing is critical; if you miss that window, you lose yield you can never get back. I spray **3 times** — herbicide, insecticide for corn borer, and one more insecticide if the aphids show up. I expect **550 kg per mu**.

For **stevia** on 13 mu, I plant the **Chengguang** variety. The buyer at the processing plant told me this variety has the highest stevioside content, and my neighbor two rows over got 275 kg per mu of dried leaf last year. Stevia drinks water like nothing else, so I will irrigate **6 times** through the season. It also needs plenty of fertilizer: **19 kg nitrogen per mu**, **12 kg phosphorus per mu**, and **14 kg potassium per mu**. I rotary till that plot deep because the roots need soft soil. I have to stay on top of pests — leaf spot and caterpillars love stevia here — so I spray **9 times** total, mixing insecticide, fungicide, and sometimes a growth regulator. I budget for **275 kg per mu** of dried leaves, which at 6 yuan per kg is good money.

For **sweet potato** on 13 mu, I use a **traditional local variety** I have been saving for a few years. Sweet potato is forgiving. I plough that field deep because the tubers need room to swell — I rent a deep plough tractor for that. I use only **3.5 kg nitrogen per mu** — too much N and you get all vines and no tubers. But I give it **8 kg phosphorus per mu** and **10 kg potassium per mu**, which helps the roots bulk up. I irrigate **2 times**, once after transplanting and once at tuber swelling. I spray **3 times** — pre-emergence herbicide, one insecticide for sweet potato weevil, and one fungicide if the leaves start spotting. I expect about **2500 kg per mu** of fresh tubers.

I know stevia and sweet potato take me over my 66 mu if I count wheat and maize separately, but the wheat and maize share the same 40 mu — one comes off, the other goes in. That's how double-cropping works here. My total input bill is high, but I would rather spend a little too much on fertilizer than risk a bad harvest. A bad year means I lose everything; wasting a bag of urea is just a cost I absorb.
